q: In the mean time, throughout all lands and in every sea, the daughter is sought in vain by her anxious mother.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ceres uses pines (Ceres's torches) (as torches)
q: She, with her two hands, sets light to some pines at the flaming Ætna

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ceres drinks barley drink (when thirsty during her search)
q: gives her, asking for water, a sweet drink which she has lately distilled[57] from parched pearled barley

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cyane is a Sicilian Nymph (the most celebrated among the Sicilian Nymphs)
q: Here was Cyane,[54] the most celebrated among the Sicilian Nymphs

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cyane is named for pool (Cyane)
q: from whose name the pool also was called

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pluto is son of Saturn
q: The son of Saturn no longer restrained his rage

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cyane is wife of Anapis (married willingly after being courted)
q: Anapis[55] also loved me. Yet I married him, courted, and not frightened {into it}, like her

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cyane's transformation into a fountain is a transformation (caused by grief and anguish)
q: through grief and anguish, dissolves into a fountain

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cyane's transformation into a fountain transforms Cyane (into a fountain)
q: is entirely dissolved into tears, and melts away into those waters, of which she had been but lately the great guardian Divinity

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Stellio is a boy (impudent and bold)
q: a boy[58] of impudent countenance and bold, stands before the Goddess, and laughs, and calls her greedy

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Stellio is transformed into a diminutive form
q: His face contracts the stains, and he bears legs where just now he was bearing arms; a tail is added to his changed limbs; and he is contracted into a diminutive form

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: newt (Stellio) is smaller than a small lizard (body speckled with various spots)
q: his size is less than {that of} a small lizard. He flies from the old woman, astounded and weeping, and trying to touch the monstrosity; and he seeks a lurking place, and has a name suited to his color, having his body speckled with various spots.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Henna has nearby Pergus (not far from its walls)
q: Not far from the walls of Henna[46] there is a lake of deep water, Pergus by name

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pluto uses Pluto's chariot (to carry away Proserpina)
q: The ravisher drives on his chariot

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: pool (Cyane) is named after Cyane
q: from whose name the pool also was called

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pluto uses Pluto's sceptre (as a weapon)
q: he threw his royal sceptre, hurled with a strong arm, into the lowest depths of the stream

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: abduction of Proserpine is performed by Pluto (by force)
q: Pluto surprises Proserpina in the fields of Henna, and carries her away by force.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: abduction of Proserpine occurs at Henna (in the fields near its walls)
q: Pluto surprises Proserpina in the fields of Henna, and carries her away by force.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ceres's search for Proserpina is a search (throughout all lands and seas)
q: Ceres goes everywhere in search of her daughter

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ceres's search for Proserpina seeks Proserpine (in vain)
q: In the mean time, throughout all lands and in every sea, the daughter is sought in vain by her anxious mother.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: transformation of Stellio is caused by Ceres (after he mocks her)
q: She is offended; and a part being not yet quaffed, the Goddess sprinkles him, as he is {thus} talking, with the barley mixed with the liquor.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: transformation of Stellio transforms Stellio (into a diminutive speckled creature)
q: His face contracts the stains, and he bears legs where just now he was bearing arms; a tail is added to his changed limbs; and he is contracted into a diminutive form

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pluto drives horses (Pluto's chariot horses) (in his chariot)
q: The ravisher drives on his chariot, and encourages his horses, called, each by his name

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pluto has horses (Pluto's chariot horses) (drawing his chariot)
q: The ravisher drives on his chariot, and encourages his horses, called, each by his name, along whose necks and manes he shakes the reins, dyed with swarthy rust.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Proserpine is daughter of Ceres
q: Ceres goes everywhere in search of her daughter

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Proserpine has companions Proserpina's companions (of the same age)
q: while, with childlike eagerness, she is filling her baskets and her bosom, and is striving to outdo {her companions} of the same age in gathering

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Henna is a city (in Sicily)
q: Henna, or Enna, was a city so exactly situated in the middle of Sicily that it was called the navel of that island.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: rape of Proserpine is associated with Henna (according to many authors)
q: Proserpine is said by many authors, besides Ovid, to have been carried away by Pluto in the vicinity of Henna; though some writers say that it took place in Attica, and others again in Asia, while the Hymn of Orpheus mentions the western coast of Spain.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Syracuse has two harbors (one much larger than the other)
q: Syracuse had two harbors, one of which was much larger than the other.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Palici is a son of Jupiter (two brothers)
q: The Palici were two brothers, sons of Jupiter and the Nymph Thalea, and, according to some, received their name from the Greek words πάλιν ἱκέσθαι, ‘to come again [to life].’

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Archias founded Syracuse (after being expelled from Corinth)
q: Archias, one of the race of the Bacchiadæ, a powerful Corinthian family, being expelled from Corinth, was said to have founded Syracuse, the capital of Sicily.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Henna is situated in Sicily (in the middle of the island)
q: Henna, or Enna, was a city so exactly situated in the middle of Sicily that it was called the navel of that island.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Corinth is called Bimaris (by Latin poets)
q: Corinth is called ‘Bimaris’ by the Latin poets, from its having the Ægean sea on one side of it, and the Ionian sea on the other.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Corinth has border Aegean Sea (on one side)
q: Corinth is called ‘Bimaris’ by the Latin poets, from its having the Ægean sea on one side of it, and the Ionian sea on the other.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Corinth has border Ionian Sea (on the other side)
q: Corinth is called ‘Bimaris’ by the Latin poets, from its having the Ægean sea on one side of it, and the Ionian sea on the other.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cyane is a companion of Proserpine (according to Claudian)
q: According to Claudian, Cyane was one of the companions of Proserpine, when she was carried off by Pluto.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Anapis mingles with Cyane (the waters of the fountain)
q: This was a river of Sicily, which, mingling with the waters of the fountain Cyane, falls into the sea at Syracuse, opposite to the island of Ortygia.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ortygia is part of Syracuse (considered part of the city)
q: This island, in which the fountain of Arethusa was situate, was separated from the isle of Sicily by a narrow strait of the sea, and communicating with the city of Syracuse by a bridge, was considered as part of it.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Arethusa is located on Ortygia (as a fountain)
q: This island, in which the fountain of Arethusa was situate, was separated from the isle of Sicily by a narrow strait of the sea, and communicating with the city of Syracuse by a bridge, was considered as part of it.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: worship of Ceres is esteemed highly (at Henna)
q: The worship of Ceres there was so highly esteemed, that ancient writers remarked, that you might easily take the whole place for one vast temple of that Goddess, and all the inhabitants for her priests.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Isis is identified with Ceres (according to Banier)
q: Banier does not agree with these suggestions of Pezeron and Le Clerc, and thinks that Ceres is no other personage than the Isis of the Egyptians, supposing that the story is founded on the following circumstance:--Greece, he says, was afflicted with famine in the reign of Erectheus, who was obliged to send to Egypt for corn, when those who went for it brought back the worship of the Deity who presided over agriculture.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: famine in Greece occurred during reign of Erectheus
q: Greece, he says, was afflicted with famine in the reign of Erectheus, who was obliged to send to Egypt for corn, when those who went for it brought back the worship of the Deity who presided over agriculture.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Erectheus sent for corn (from Egypt during the famine)
q: Greece, he says, was afflicted with famine in the reign of Erectheus, who was obliged to send to Egypt for corn, when those who went for it brought back the worship of the Deity who presided over agriculture.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ceres has worship worship of Ceres (highly esteemed at Henna)
q: The worship of Ceres there was so highly esteemed, that ancient writers remarked, that you might easily take the whole place for one vast temple of that Goddess, and all the inhabitants for her priests.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Triptolemus established worship of Ceres (in Eleusis)
q: Triptolemus established her worship in Eleusis, and there instituted the mysteries which he had brought over from Egypt.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Triptolemus instituted Eleusinian mysteries (in Eleusis; brought from Egypt)
q: Triptolemus established her worship in Eleusis, and there instituted the mysteries which he had brought over from Egypt.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Eleusinian mysteries originated in Egypt (brought over by Triptolemus)
q: Triptolemus established her worship in Eleusis, and there instituted the mysteries which he had brought over from Egypt.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ceres can protect from the famine (as a Goddess)
q: The evils which the Athenians had suffered by the famine, and the dread of again incurring the same calamity, made them willingly embrace the rites of a Goddess whom they believed able to protect them from it.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Eleusis is located in Attica
q: Upon this, Ceres went to Greece, in search of her daughter; and, resting at Eleusis, in Attica, she heard that the ship in which her daughter was carried away had sailed westward.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Aidoneus is a king of Epirus (according to Le Clerc)
q: Le Clerc, on the other hand, thinks that it was not Pluto that carried away Proserpine, but Aidoneus, king of Epirus, or Orcus king of the Molossians.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Epirus is compared to Infernal Regions (figuratively, because it was situated very low)
q: Epirus too, which was situate very low, may have been figuratively described as the Infernal Regions; for which reason, the journeys of Theseus and Hercules into Epirus may have been spoken of as descents into the Stygian abodes.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pluto is confounded with Aidoneus (because of the similarity of their realms)
q: Aidoneus is supposed to have wrought mines in his kingdom, and, as the entrance into it was over a river called Acheron, that prince has often been confounded with Pluto;

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Infernal Regions is associated with Pluto (as his supposed realm)
q: The situation of his kingdom, which lay very low, comparatively with Greece, and which the ancients believed to be covered with eternal darkness, gave rise to the fable, that Pluto had got Hell for his share;

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Proserpine is also called Pherephata
q: Cicero and Strabo agree with Ovid in telling us that Proserpine, the only daughter of Ceres, whom other writers name Pherephata, was walking in the adjacent meadows, and gathering flowers with her companions; upon which, certain pirates seized her, and, placing her in a chariot, carried her to the seaside, whence they embarked for Epirus.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Jupiter decided dispute between Ceres and Pluto (according to the allegorical explanation)
q: Jupiter was said to have decided the difference between Ceres and Pluto, because the earth again became covered with crops.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: transformation of Stellio is attributed to Poet’s fancy (possibly without historical foundation)
q: It is very possible that the story of the transformation of Stellio into a newt may have had no other foundation than the Poet’s fancy.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Proserpine is a daughter of Ceres (only daughter)
q: Cicero and Strabo agree with Ovid in telling us that Proserpine, the only daughter of Ceres, whom other writers name Pherephata, was walking in the adjacent meadows, and gathering flowers with her companions; upon which, certain pirates seized her, and, placing her in a chariot, carried her to the seaside, whence they embarked for Epirus.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ceres is a mother of Proserpine (only daughter)
q: Cicero and Strabo agree with Ovid in telling us that Proserpine, the only daughter of Ceres, whom other writers name Pherephata, was walking in the adjacent meadows, and gathering flowers with her companions; upon which, certain pirates seized her, and, placing her in a chariot, carried her to the seaside, whence they embarked for Epirus.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pluto is a God of the Earth (name Dis)
q: Pluto is here called ‘Dis.’ This name was given to him as the God of the Earth, from the bowels of which riches are dug up.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pluto is also called Dis (as God of the Earth)
q: Pluto is here called ‘Dis.’ This name was given to him as the God of the Earth, from the bowels of which riches are dug up.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ceres is a Goddess
q: The Goddess makes her complaint to Jupiter

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Proserpine is subject to the law of the Destinies (concerning return to the upper world)
q: for thus has it been provided by the law of the Destinies.”

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Jupiter is a father (of Proserpine)
q: I have come, Jupiter, as a suppliant to thee, both for my own offspring and for thine.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Jupiter is brother of Pluto
q: how great a thing is it to be the brother of Jupiter!

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Arethusa is a Nymph (of the Alpheian waters)
q: Then the Alpheian Nymph[62] raised her head from out of the Elean waters

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Arethusa is native to Pisa
q: Pisa is my native place

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Arethusa derives birth from Elis
q: and from Elis do I derive my birth.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Arethusa inhabits Sicily (as a stranger)
q: As a stranger do I inhabit Sicily

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Arethusa has abode in Ortygia (after being carried through the waters of spacious seas)
q: and have been carried to Ortygia, through the waters of seas so spacious

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Arethusa passes under world (through its lowest caverns)
q: The pervious earth affords me a passage, and, carried beneath its lowest caverns

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ceres is mother of Proserpine
q: O thou mother of the virgin sought over the whole world

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Arethusa flows through Styx (beneath the earth)
q: While, then, I was running under the earth, along the Stygian stream

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Arethusa sees Proserpine (in the world of darkness)
q: thy Proserpine was there beheld by my eyes.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ascalaphus is a son (of Orphne and Acheron)
q: whom Orphne, by no means the most obscure among the Nymphs of Avernus,[68] is said once to have borne to her own Acheron within {his} dusky caves

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ascalaphus is a informer (against Proserpine)
q: He beheld {this}, and cruelly prevented her return by his discovery.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ascalaphus is transformed into an accursed bird (as punishment)
q: The Queen of Erebus grieved, and changed the informer into an accursed bird

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ascalaphus has head that becomes larger
q: his head becomes larger, his long nails bend inwards, and with difficulty can he move the wings that spring through his sluggish arms.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: owl is a bird (obscene and ominous)
q: He becomes an obscene bird, the foreboder of approaching woe, a lazy owl, a direful omen to mortals.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: owl forebodes approaching woe (to mortals)
q: He becomes an obscene bird, the foreboder of approaching woe, a lazy owl, a direful omen to mortals.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Sicily does not deserve it (against its will)
q: This land does not deserve it; and against its will it gave a path for {the commission of} the outrage.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ceres searches for Proserpine (throughout the whole world)
q: Ceres proceeds in a fruitless search for her daughter over the whole earth

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: agriculture and fertility is ruined in Sicily (after Ceres’s anger)
q: The fertility of the soil, famed over the wide world, lies in ruin

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: pomegranate contains pomegranate seeds (within its pale rind)
q: she had plucked a pomegranate[65] from the bending tree, and had chewed in her mouth seven grains[66] taken from the pale rind

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: the pomegranate eating affects Proserpine’s return to the upper world (by preventing it)
q: He beheld {this}, and cruelly prevented her return by his discovery.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: abduction of Proserpine occurs in Sicily (against Sicily’s will)
q: This land does not deserve it; and against its will it gave a path for {the commission of} the outrage.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Sirens are daughters of Acheloüs (with maiden faces and bird-like limbs)
q: Whence have you, daughters of Acheloüs,[70] feathers and the feet of birds, since you have the faces of maidens

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Sirens possess feathers (after transformation)
q: you wished to be able, on the support of your wings, to hover over the waves, and you found the Gods propitious, and saw your limbs grow yellow with feathers suddenly formed.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Sirens possess feet of birds (after transformation)
q: Whence have you, daughters of Acheloüs,[70] feathers and the feet of birds, since you have the faces of maidens

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Sirens retain human voice (despite their transformation)
q: your virgin countenance and your human voice {still} remained.”

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ceres possesses chariot
q: she departed in her chariot into the ætherial air

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Sirens seek Proserpine (throughout the whole world)
q: After you had sought her in vain throughout the whole world

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ceres is associated with corn (as its giver)
q: calls them ungrateful, and not worthy of the gifts of corn

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Proserpine is a daughter (of Ceres and Jupiter)
q: I have come, Jupiter, as a suppliant to thee, both for my own offspring and for thine.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Proserpine is a queen (in the world of darkness)
q: but still {she is} a queen, and the most ennobled {female} in the world of darkness

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Proserpine is spouse of Pluto (the Infernal King)
q: still, too, is she the powerful spouse of the Infernal King.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Proserpine eats pomegranate seeds (seven grains)
q: she had plucked a pomegranate[65] from the bending tree, and had chewed in her mouth seven grains[66] taken from the pale rind

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Proserpine’s girdle is a fastening around the loins
q: The zone, or girdle, a fastening round the loins, was much worn by both sexes among the ancients.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Arethusa informs Ceres (of Proserpine’s fate)
q: Ovid here makes Arethusa the discoverer to Ceres of the fate of her daughter.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ceres learns from Arethusa (the fate of her daughter)
q: Ovid here makes Arethusa the discoverer to Ceres of the fate of her daughter.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: pomegranate is avoided by Thesmophoriazusae (during the rites of Ceres)
q: It was for this reason that the Thesmophoriazusæ, in the performance of the rites of Ceres, were especially careful not to taste the pomegranate.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ascalaphus is a son of Acheron (according to Apollodorus)
q: He was the son of Acheron, by the Nymph Orphne, or Gorgyra, according to Apollodorus.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ascalaphus is a courtier of Pluto (according to the explanation)
q: he was one of the courtiers of Pluto

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ascalaphus advises Pluto (to carry away Proserpine)
q: who, having advised his master to carry away Proserpine

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ascalaphus obstructs Ceres (in restoring Proserpine)
q: did all that lay in his power to obstruct the endeavors of Ceres, and hinder the restoration of her daughter

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ascalaphus is transformed into owl (for his unseasonable discovery)
q: she changed him into an owl, called ὦτον.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ascalaphus is transformed into newt (Stellio) (in another version of the story)
q: Some writers state that he was changed into a lizard, which the Greeks call ‘Ascalabos,’

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ascalaphus’s punishment and transformation is based on death in Pluto’s mines (possibly)
q: It has also been suggested that the story of his change into an owl was based on the circumstance that he was the overseer of the mines of Pluto, in which he perished, removed from the light of day.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Proserpine’s girdle holds up tunic (chief use)
q: the chief use of it was for holding up the tunic, and keeping it from dragging on the ground.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Infernal Regions has threshold Avernus (in mythological geography)
q: Being feigned to be the mouth, or threshold, of the Infernal Regions

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Infernal Regions contains Phlegethon (as a burning river)
q: This was a burning river of the Infernal Regions

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: treaty concerning Proserpine divides residence between world (nine months with Ceres and three with Pluto, according to Apollodorus)
q: the terms of the treaty respecting Proserpine were, that she should stay on earth nine months with Ceres, and three with Pluto, in the Infernal Regions.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: treaty concerning Proserpine divides residence between Infernal Regions (three months with Pluto, according to Apollodorus)
q: the terms of the treaty respecting Proserpine were, that she should stay on earth nine months with Ceres, and three with Pluto, in the Infernal Regions.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: treaty concerning Proserpine has alternative division six months (to Ceres and six to Pluto according to other writers)
q: Other writers divide the time equally; six months to Ceres, and six to Pluto.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Sirens are daughters of Acheloüs (according to the myth)
q: The Sirens were said to be the daughters of the river Acheloüs and of one of the Muses

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Sirens are daughters of Muses (one of the Muses; according to the myth)
q: The Sirens were said to be the daughters of the river Acheloüs and of one of the Muses, either Calliope, Melpomene, or Terpsichore.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Sirens are transformed into birds (to search for Proserpine)
q: Ovid, probably, feigned that the Sirens begged the Gods to change them into birds, that they might seek for Proserpine

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Proserpine’s girdle holds money (sometimes, among men)
q: The girdle was used sometimes by men to hold money instead of a purse

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ceres's search for Proserpina is conducted by Sirens (according to the explanation)
q: the Sirens begged the Gods to change them into birds, that they might seek for Proserpine
